Homework 2

Introduction

In this analysis, we will apply supervised learning tools for both classification and advanced regression. To do this, we will use a dataset which documents the factors affecting the agricultural yield of a piece of land, such as rain, irrigation, fertilization, etc.

We will use the agricultural yield as both a categorical and a numerical target variable, dividing it into high and low yield for the classification.

Data preprocessing

Load the data

We load the children anemia dataset.

rm(list=ls()) # delete all previous data on the environment
training = read.csv("agricultural_yield_train.csv")
testing = read.csv("agricultural_yield_test.csv")

set.seed(123) # We set the seed to obtain consistent results

Libraries

We load all the libraries needed for this project.

library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(mice)
library(VIM)
library(GGally)
library(MASS)
library(glmnet)
library(e1071) 
library(rpart)
library(pROC)
library(class)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(fastDummies)

Feature engineering

At first, we thought about changing the seed variety variable (a numerical variable where 1 is a high yield seed variety and 0 a low yield seed variety) into a factor variable. However, this stops us from being able to use ggcorr() and seeing its relationship with the target variable, so we decided against it.


# We use the median as a threshold for a new variable called Yield which will be used for the classification. This variable will have two levels, high and low to allow glm classification. 

# We create separate training / testing datasets for the classification and the regression.

trainingCls = training
testingCls = testing

# We calculate the median using both the training and testing sets.
med = (4*median(training$Yield_kg_per_hectare) + median(testing$Yield_kg_per_hectare))/ 5

trainingCls$Yield = as.factor(ifelse(trainingCls[["Yield_kg_per_hectare"]] > med, "High", "Low"))
testingCls$Yield = as.factor(ifelse(testingCls[["Yield_kg_per_hectare"]] > med, "High", "Low"))

trainingCls <- trainingCls %>%  dplyr::select(-Yield_kg_per_hectare)
testingCls <- testingCls %>%  dplyr::select(-Yield_kg_per_hectare)

NA

We check if there are NA values.

which(is.na(training), arr.ind=TRUE)
     row col
which(is.na(testing), arr.ind=TRUE)
     row col

There are no NA values.

Visualization

We will use a correlation table to see the relations between the different variables:

ggcorr(training, label = T)

As we can see, the most important variables are seed variety and the irrigation schedule, while soil quality and the number of sunny days are far less important. We can also see that none of the variables that we will use to predict the yield have any correlation with each other, meaning that it will be futile to try to combine them into other variables to thus improve the performance of any model.

Let’s plot the different variables for the classification:

# Numeric vs categorical plot:
ggplot(trainingCls, aes(Irrigation_Schedule)) + geom_density(aes(group=Yield, colour=Yield, fill=Yield), alpha=0.1) +xlab("Fertilizer amount")


ggplot(trainingCls, aes(Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare)) + geom_density(aes(group=Yield, colour=Yield, fill=Yield), alpha=0.1) +xlab("Fertilizer amount")


ggplot(trainingCls, aes(Sunny_Days)) + geom_density(aes(group=Yield, colour=Yield, fill=Yield), alpha=0.1) +xlab("Fertilizer amount") # The distributions are almost the same.

And for the regression:

training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Rainfall_mm)) + geom_density(fill="navyblue")


training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Yield_kg_per_hectare/Irrigation_Schedule)) + geom_density(fill="navyblue") # Not much variance, indicating a linear relationship


training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Irrigation_Schedule, y=Yield_kg_per_hectare)) + geom_point(color="navyblue")


training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare, y=Yield_kg_per_hectare)) + geom_point(color="navyblue")


training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Rainfall_mm, y=Yield_kg_per_hectare)) + geom_point(color="navyblue") # Negative slope


training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Soil_Quality, y=Yield_kg_per_hectare)) + geom_point(color="navyblue") # Barely any correlation, too much noise


training %>% ggplot(aes(x=Sunny_Days, y=Yield_kg_per_hectare)) + geom_point(color="navyblue") # Barely any correlation, too much noise

Classification

Bayes Classifiers

For the classification, we are going to start with the Bayes classifiers LDA and QDA, which we are going to compare to each other to obtain the best model which maximizes the accuracy. Our measure of success will be the accuracy, since by default it takes into account both false negatives and true positives unlike the specificity and sensitivity.

LDA

lda.model <- lda(Yield ~ ., data=trainingCls)

probability_lda = predict(lda.model, newdata=testingCls)$posterior

prediction_lda = predict(lda.model, newdata=testingCls)$class
head(probability_lda)

prediction_qda = predict(qda.model, newdata=testingCls)$class

As we can see, the LDA model is more accurate, with an accuracy slightly above 90%. Nonetheless, we will try other models to see if they are better.

Logistic regression

Because we have binary classification, we can use the standard glm function in R:

logit.model <- glm(Yield ~ ., family=binomial(link='logit'), data=trainingCls)
summary(logit.model)

Penalized logistic regression

When there is a high number of dimensions, it is better to use a penalized version with glmnet.

logit.model <- glmnet(as.matrix(trainingCls),trainingCls$Yield, family=c("binomial"), alpha=0, lambda=0.01)

As we can see, the accuracy has slightly improved over the normal logistic regression model. The previous alpha and lambda are hyper-parameters which we will try to optimize.

Variable importance

We can use another method for penalized regression, which allows us to see the importance of each variable, however, since it does not improve the accuracy compared to a normal logistic regression model, we will not use it for anything else.

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE, 
                     verboseIter=T)

lrFit <- train(Yield ~ ., 
               method = "glmnet",
               tuneGrid = expand.grid(alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), lambda = seq(0, .1, 0.02)),
               metric = "Kappa",
               data = trainingCls,
               preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
               trControl = ctrl)

The ROC curve

The ROC curve shows true positives vs false positives in relation with different thresholds:

  • y-axis = Sensitivity (TP)
  • x-axis = Specificity (1-FP)

probability = predict(logit.model,as.matrix(testingCls), type='response') 
Warning: NAs introducidos por coerción
roc.glm <- roc(testingCls$Yield,probability) 
Setting levels: control = High, case = Low
Warning: Deprecated use a matrix as predictor. Unexpected results may be produced, please pass a numeric vector.Setting direction: controls < cases
auc(roc.glm)
Area under the curve: 0.9774

Economic impact

We will adjust our model taking into account that a farmer’s prediction about whether there will be a high or low yield will affect that farmer’s profit depending on the outcome (because that farmer will buy more / less fertilizer, irrigation, seeds, etc). Our objective is to maximize a farmer’s profit.

Profit matrix:

Prediction/Reference High yield Low yield
Predicted high yield 10000 -1000
Predicted low yield 5000 2000

Profit table as a vector:

profit.unit <- c(10000, 5000, -1000, 2000)

What is the expected profit using our last model as a basis for predicting future yields?

CM = confusionMatrix(factor(prediction), testingCls$Yield)$table
profit = sum(as.vector(CM)*profit.unit)/sum(CM)
profit
[1] 5573.75

Cost-sensitive classifier

We will see if a different value of the threshold will give us a better expected profit (keep in mind that the code takes a few minutes to run).


profit.i = matrix(NA, nrow = 100, ncol = 10) 
# 20 replicates for training/testing sets for each of the 10 values of threshold  
j <- 0 
for (threshold in seq(0.05,0.5,0.05)){      
  
  j <- j + 1   
  cat(j)   
  for(i in 1:100){          
    
    lrFit <- train(Yield ~ ., data=trainingCls, method = "glmnet",                    tuneGrid = data.frame(alpha = 0.3, lambda = 0), preProcess = c("center", "scale"),                    
                   trControl = trainControl(method = "none", classProbs = TRUE))          
    
    lrProb = predict(lrFit, testingCls, type="prob")     
    lrPred = rep("High", nrow(testingCls))     
    lrPred[which(lrProb[,2] > threshold)] = "Low"          
    CM = confusionMatrix(factor(lrPred), testingCls$Yield)$table     
    profit = sum(as.vector(CM)*profit.unit)/sum(CM)     
    profit          
    profit.i[i,j] <- profit        
  
  } 
}  
1

We do not obtain a greater profit that with our initial model, so we will not change the threshold.

Decision trees

We will try machine learning models to see if they perform better than the previous models.

library(rpart)  
# Hyper-parameters 
control = rpart.control(minsplit = 50, maxdepth = 15, cp=0.01)  
# Parameters chosen to try to maximize the accuracy
# minsplit: minimum number of observations in a node before before a split 
# maxdepth: maximum depth of any node of the final tree # cp: degree of complexity, the smaller the more branches 

model = Yield ~. 
dtFit <- rpart(model, data=trainingCls, method = "class", control = control) 
summary(dtFit)

Visualization:

library(rpart.plot) 
Warning: package ‘rpart.plot’ was built under R version 4.3.2
rpart.plot(dtFit, digits=3)

To create a full tree, we set the complexity parameter cp to 0 (split even if it does not improve the tree) and we set the minimum number of observations in a node needed to split to the smallest value of 2:

control = rpart.control(minsplit = 50, maxdepth = 15, cp=0.001) # Parameters chosen to try to maximize the accuracy
dtFit <- rpart(model, data=trainingCls, method = "class", control = control)  
rpart.plot(dtFit, digits = 3)

Prediction:

dtPred <- predict(dtFit, testingCls, type = "class")  
dtProb <- predict(dtFit, testingCls, type = "prob") 
threshold = 0.2 
dtPred = rep("High", nrow(testingCls)) 
dtPred[which(dtProb[,2] > threshold)] = "Low"

CM = confusionMatrix(factor(dtPred), testingCls$Yield)$table
accuracy = sum(diag(CM)) / sum(CM)
CM
          Reference
Prediction High  Low
      High 1549  133
      Low   400 1918
accuracy
[1] 0.86675

The accuracy is much lower than that obtained with glm and glmnet.

Random Forest


rf.train <- randomForest(Yield ~., data=trainingCls,                      ntree=200,mtry=6,importance=TRUE, do.trace=T)

# Parameters chosen to try to maximize the accuracy
# mtry: number of variables randomly sampled as candidates at each split 
# ntree: number of trees to grow 
# cutoff: cutoff probabilities in majority vote

Prediction:

rf.pred <- predict(rf.train, newdata=testingCls) 
confusionMatrix(rf.pred, testingCls$Yield)

While the accuracy from the random forest model is higher than that obtained with previous machine learning tree algorithms, it is still inferior to the accuracy obtained with glm and glmnet.

summary(linFit)

Multiple regression

linFit <- lm(Yield_kg_per_hectare ~ Seed_Variety + Irrigation_Schedule + Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare + Soil_Quality + Sunny_Days + Rainfall_mm, data=training)
summary(linFit)

'
Examples of alternative models with a lower or equal R^2:

linFit <- lm(log(Yield_kg_per_hectare) ~ Seed_Variety + Irrigation_Schedule + Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare + Soil_Quality + Sunny_Days + Rainfall_mm, data=training)

linFit <- lm(Yield_kg_per_hectare ~ Seed_Variety + Irrigation_Schedule + Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare + Soil_Quality + log(Sunny_Days) + Rainfall_mm, data=training)
'

Though using different models, we have concluded that the best linear regression model includes all variables, without using logarithms to find exponential relationships.

Prediction

predictions <- predict(linFit, newdata=testing) 
cor(testing$Yield_kg_per_hectare, predictions)^2 
[1] 0.9356143
RMSE <- sqrt(mean((predictions - testing$Yield_kg_per_hectare)^2)) 
RMSE
[1] 50.62647

Seems reasonable. R2 in testing is the same to that in training.

Now we need to try some advanced regression models: statistical learning + machine learning.

A benchmark

mean(training$Yield_kg_per_hectare)

ModelF = Yield_kg_per_hectare ~ Seed_Variety + Irrigation_Schedule + Soil_Quality + Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare + Sunny_Days + Rainfall_mm

Ridge regression

Let’s use first the original glmnet package.

glmnet

The package, written originally in Fortran, does not allow for R formulas, hence we need to transform a model into a matrix format.

library(glmnet)  

# X matrix 
X = model.matrix(ModelF, data=training)[,-1]  # skip column of ones  

# y variable 
y = training$Yield_kg_per_hectare

Now we need to define a grid for the penalty hyper-parameter lambda.

grid = seq(0, .1, length = 100)  # a 100-size grid for lambda (rho in slides)

We estimate the ridge regression for all the penalties defined in the grid. The algorithm is extremely fast.

ridge.mod = glmnet(X, y, alpha=0, lambda=grid)  # alpha=0 for ridge regression

Ridge regression is shrinking only beta’s associated with variables, not \(\beta_0\).

For each of the 100 values of rho (lambda), there are 10 estimated parameters.

Solution path:

plot(ridge.mod, xvar="lambda")

How do we select the optimal hyper-parameter?

ridge.cv = cv.glmnet(X, y, type.measure="mse", alpha=0) 
plot(ridge.cv)

The lowest point in the curve indicates the optimal lambda: the log value of lambda that best minimised the error in cross-validation.

opt.lambda <- ridge.cv$lambda.min  
opt.lambda
[1] 13.7539

lambda.1se is recommended to estimate the betas.

lambda.index <- which(ridge.cv$lambda == ridge.cv$lambda.1se)  
beta.ridge <- ridge.cv$glmnet.fit$beta[, lambda.index]  
beta.ridge
                    Seed_Variety              Irrigation_Schedule 
                     281.3399256                       46.8588729 
                    Soil_Quality Fertilizer_Amount_kg_per_hectare 
                       1.4439985                        0.7567707 
                      Sunny_Days                      Rainfall_mm 
                       1.8665936                       -0.4735693

Prediction:

X.test = model.matrix(ModelF, data=testing)[,-1]  # skip column of ones

ridge.pred = predict(ridge.cv$glmnet.fit, s=opt.lambda, newx=X.test)

To visualize the performance, we can use the postResample function in caret.

y.test = testing$Yield_kg_per_hectare
postResample(pred = ridge.pred,  obs = y.test)
      RMSE   Rsquared        MAE 
51.8569112  0.9356189 41.4899450

The performance is higher than with all previous methods.

Let’s do it now with caret.

caret

# the grid for lambda 
ridge_grid <- expand.grid(lambda = seq(0, .1, length = 100))  

# train 
ridge_tune <- train(ModelF, data = training,                     
                    method='ridge',                     
                    preProc=c('scale','center'),                     
                    tuneGrid = ridge_grid,                     
                    trControl=ctrl)  

# the best tune 
ridge_tune$bestTune  

# prediction 
test_results$ridge <- predict(ridge_tune, testing)

postResample(pred = test_results$ridge,  obs = test_results$Yield_kg_per_hectare)

Therefore, we have found that the best regression model (the one with the highest R^2) involves tuning hyper parameters with glmnet.

Conclusion

In conclusion, we have found that both in the classification and in the linear regression, the best model uses glmnet while tuning the hyperparameters (the threshold in the classification and lambda in the linear regression). In fact, we have used those models to achieve impressive results capable of predicting the yield based on the rest of the variables, whch could be used by farmers to maximize their profits.
